title: Detection and quantification of extracellular microRNAs in murine biofluids
author: Roberts, Coenen-Stass, et al.
materials: i. Export RDML file from qPCR software.
iii. ‘Extract all’ from the new .zip file.
xiv. Click ‘OK’ to load the data.
xv. Click ‘determine baselines’ to initiate analysis.

steps.title: Prepare RNase‑free environment
steps.instruction: Wear clean gloves, use RNase‑free plasticware and barrier pipette tips; keep all RNA solutions on ice to minimise degradation.

steps.title: Aliquot and adjust biofluid
steps.instruction: Aliquot a user‑defined volume of biofluid (typically 50 µl, but as little as 10 µl can be used) into a clean RNase‑free 1.7 ml microcentrifuge tube and adjust the total volume to 200 µl with nuclease‑free water.

steps.title: Add TRIzol LS
steps.instruction: Add 600 µl of TRIzol LS reagent to the tube and mix by vortexing for 10 seconds.

steps.title: Add external spike‑in
steps.instruction: Add 3 µl of 5 nM external spike‑in control to each sample and vortex for 10 seconds.

steps.title: Add optional carrier RNA
steps.instruction: OPTIONAL: Add 1 µl of 1 µg/µl MS2 bacteriophage carrier RNA solution to improve extraction efficiency.

steps.title: Incubate TRIzol mixture
steps.instruction: Incubate the TRIzol LS/biofluid mixture for 5 minutes at room temperature.

steps.title: Add chloroform
steps.instruction: Add 160 µl of chloroform to each sample and vortex for 15 seconds.

steps.title: Incubate after chloroform
steps.instruction: Incubate the TRIzol LS/chloroform mixture for 15 minutes at room temperature.

steps.title: Phase‑separation centrifugation
steps.instruction: Centrifuge the samples at 12 000 g for 15 minutes at 4 °C. The mixture separates into three phases; the clear aqueous top phase contains the RNA.

steps.title: Transfer aqueous phase
steps.instruction: Transfer the aqueous phase to a clean 1.7 ml microcentrifuge tube.

steps.title: Optional phenolic re‑hydration
steps.instruction: OPTIONAL: Add an additional volume of nuclease‑free water to the phenolic phase, vortex, repeat phase separation, pool the aqueous layers and proceed with isopropanol precipitation to maximise RNA recovery.

steps.title: Add glycogen (critical)
steps.instruction: CRITICAL STEP: Add 1 µl RNase‑free glycogen to each sample to ensure efficient RNA precipitation.

steps.title: Isopropanol precipitation
steps.instruction: Add 400 µl of isopropanol, vortex the samples, and incubate for 10 minutes at room temperature. PAUSE POINT: Samples may be precipitated overnight if required.

steps.title: Pellet RNA
steps.instruction: Centrifuge at 12 000 g for 10 minutes at 4 °C; a gel‑like pellet forms at the bottom. Discard the supernatant.

steps.title: Ethanol wash
steps.instruction: Wash the RNA pellet with 1 ml of 75 % ethanol, vortex to resuspend, then centrifuge at 7 500 g for 5 minutes at 4 °C. Discard the ethanol wash.

steps.title: Remove residual ethanol
steps.instruction: Pulse‑spin the samples, remove residual ethanol with a narrow pipette tip, discard the supernatant and air‑dry the pellet for 10 minutes at room temperature.

steps.title: Resuspend RNA
steps.instruction: Dissolve the RNA pellet in 30 µl RNase‑free water, mix by pipetting, and incubate for 10 minutes at 55 °C.

steps.title: Store RNA
steps.instruction: PAUSE POINT: Store the resuspended RNA at –80 °C until ready for reverse transcription.

steps.title: Inspect amplification curves
steps.instruction: Inspect raw qPCR data to ensure all reactions show sigmoidal or parabolic amplification curves; adjust fluorescence background manually if curves are abnormal.

steps.title: Check negative controls
steps.instruction: Verify that negligible amplification is observed in the no‑template control (NTC) and reverse‑transcription negative (RT‑) wells.

steps.title: Check melt profiles
steps.instruction: If SYBR‑Green (intercalating dye) was used, examine melt curves for a single, expected peak; exclude reactions with multiple or atypical peaks.

steps.title: Set plot axis and threshold
steps.instruction: Set the y‑axis of the amplification plot to log scale and adjust the threshold to lie within the log‑linear phase of amplification for all reactions; standardise the threshold across plates for comparability.

steps.title: Check PCR efficiency
steps.instruction: If a standard curve was prepared, confirm that the estimated PCR efficiency lies between 80 % and 110 %.

steps.title: Validate linear range
steps.instruction: Ensure all samples fall within the linear range of the standard curve; flag any out‑of‑range samples. Reactions amplifying after the lowest standard are marked ‘Not Quantified’ or ‘Not Detected’.

steps.title: Assess template inhibition
steps.instruction: When a serial dilution of template cDNA was used for the standard curve, verify that high‑standard reactions show no inhibition; exclude samples that amplify in the problematic range.

steps.title: Export data to Excel
steps.instruction: Export the analysis results (Cq values, amounts in arbitrary units or copies, and the chosen quantification method) from the qPCR software to Microsoft Excel or an equivalent spreadsheet.

steps.title: Determine PCR efficiency (LinRegPCR)
steps.instruction: Use LinRegPCR to calculate individual reaction efficiencies:

substeps.instruction: i. Export the RDML file from the qPCR software.
ii. Rename the file extension from .rdml to .zip (ensure Windows shows file extensions).
iii. Extract all files from the .zip archive.
iv. Rename rdml_data.xml to my_experiment.xml.
v. Re‑zip my_experiment.xml using 7‑zip.
vi. Rename the new archive to my_experiment.rdml.
vii. Open LinRegPCR software.
viii. Choose File → Read from RDML.
ix. Select ‘Hydrolysis Probe’ as Monitoring Chemistry.
x. Select ‘ss cDNA’ for Amplification of.
xi. Select ‘cDNA sequence’ for Probe is targeting.
xii. Choose ‘No’ for Data are baseline corrected.
xiii. Click Open RDML File and browse to my_experiment.rdml.
xiv. Click OK to load the data.
xv. Click ‘determine baselines’ to start analysis.
xvi. When analysis finishes, choose File → Save to Excel (Excel must be open) and click OK.
xvii. The PCR efficiency for each reaction appears in column B; the mean efficiency for the plate appears in column G.

steps.title: Prepare cDNA standard curve
steps.instruction: Prepare a serial dilution (2‑ to 10‑fold as required) of the reverse‑transcription product (from step 34) and run qPCR as described in steps 35‑42, assigning the appropriate wells as standards.

steps.title: Estimate efficiency from standard curve
steps.instruction: Plot Cq values against log10(cDNA amount) for the diluted standards; calculate the gradient. A gradient of –3.32 corresponds to 100 % efficiency (E = 2). Compute efficiency using E = 10^(–1/gradient).

steps.title: Pfaffl analysis
steps.instruction: Perform Pfaffl analysis on exported Cq values:

substeps.instruction: i. Use the PCR efficiency values obtained in step 51.
ii. For each reaction, calculate the amount of starting material as (PCR efficiency)^(–Cq).
iii. Divide the gene‑of‑interest amount by the reference gene amount to obtain normalized values.
iv. Scale the data by setting the mean normalized value of the control group to 1 (divide each normalized value by the control mean).

steps.title: Absolute quantification (synthetic standards)
steps.instruction: Generate a standard curve with synthetic RNA oligonucleotides and quantify miRNA copies:

substeps.instruction: i. Prepare 5 nM stocks of each synthetic oligonucleotide (≈3.01 × 10^9 miRNA copies/µl).
ii. Add 3 µl of each 5 nM oligonucleotide to a fresh 1.7 ml tube.
iii. Bring the volume to 1 ml with nuclease‑free water (or 20 ng/µl yeast tRNA as required), yielding ≈9.03 × 10^6 miRNA copies/µl.
iv. Create a 10‑fold dilution series (5 steps) using 20 ng/µl yeast tRNA as diluent.
v. Use 5 µl of each diluted oligonucleotide/tRNA solution per 20 µl reverse‑transcriptase reaction.
vi. Add 1.33 µl of the resulting cDNA to each 20 µl qPCR reaction (top standard contains ~3 × 10^6 copies).
vii. Reverse‑transcribe the standards as described in steps 30‑34 and run qPCR as described in steps 35‑42.
viii. Determine copies per sample by comparing sample Cq values to the standard curve.
